Rebbetzin Denah Weinberg: A Legacy of Greatness, Education and Women's Empowerment
A Life's Work of Outreach and Influence: The Work, Torah Teaching and Legacy of Rebbetzin Denah Weinberg
The text surveys the life story and teaching of Rebbetzin Denah Weinberg, a key figure in the world of teshuvah (return to observance) and of Orthodox women's education, who founded the EYAHT midrasha in Jerusalem. The survey emphasizes her unique educational vision, which called on women to abandon mediocrity in favor of striving for excellence and spiritual greatness, while combining in-depth Torah study with the sanctification of family life and motherhood. The text presents the main points of her thought, which include belief in precise individual Divine providence, the importance of mutual respect in marriage, and the view of everyday tasks as exalted holy service. In sum, the source portrays the Rebbetzin as a leader who succeeded in bridging uncompromising Torah intellectualism with human warmth, thereby leaving a living legacy that continues to shape the identity of Jewish women throughout the world.
A Life's Work of Outreach and Influence: The Work, Torah Teaching and Legacy of Rebbetzin Denah Weinberg
Rebbetzin Denah (Dina) Weinberg (1938–2023) was one of the pioneers of the world of teshuvah and of Orthodox women's education in the second half of the twentieth century and the beginning of the twenty-first century.[1, 2] She founded and headed the EYAHT midrasha in Jerusalem, an academic Torah institution that has produced more than 2,000 graduates throughout the world.[1, 3] Beyond her institutional work, Rebbetzin Weinberg developed a unique educational and intellectual teaching that focused on striving for excellence and spiritual greatness, on a deep appreciation of the holiness of the home and of motherhood, and on establishing relations of mutual respect in married life.[2, 3] Her figure combined uncompromising intellectualism with human and familial warmth, and she deeply influenced the shaping of the identity of many Jewish women in our generation.[4]
Biographical and Family Background
Rebbetzin Denah Weinberg was born in the Far Rockaway neighborhood of Queens, New York, to Albert (Rabbi Yaakov Yitzchak Goldman, who later was active in Pawtucket, Rhode Island) and Esther Goldman.[1, 3] She grew up in a home that produced generations of self-sacrificing devotion to Torah and education.[1] In February 1958 she married Rabbi Noah Weinberg in New York.[1] Shortly after their marriage they settled in Jerusalem, where they established a large family and raised twelve children—eight sons and four daughters.[1, 2, 4] One of their sons, Rabbi Hillel Weinberg, even temporarily succeeded his father as head of the "Aish HaTorah" yeshiva.[1]
In 1974, after a formative encounter with five tourists at the Western Wall, her husband, Rabbi Noah Weinberg, founded the "Aish HaTorah" educational center in the Old City of Jerusalem.[3] This enterprise quickly became a worldwide network of outreach and educational institutions.[3, 5] Rebbetzin Weinberg was a full partner in her husband's vision.[4] In the years when her husband traveled for long periods throughout the world to raise resources and establish branches, the Rebbetzin bore the burden of raising the children and running the household without a trace of complaint.[4] The Rebbetzin's home was described as a "Shabbat palace," an open and warm place where searching souls from every corner of the world found refuge and guidance.[4]
After her husband's death in 2009, the Rebbetzin continued to lead and teach.[1] She passed away in Jerusalem on 12 March 2023, at the age of 85, leaving behind a rich educational legacy and generations of students who owe her their spiritual world.[1, 2]
The Meaning of the Name and the Comparison with the Biblical Figure of Dinah
The midrashic analysis of the name of Rebbetzin Denah (Dina) reveals parallel lines with the figure of the biblical Dinah, the daughter of Jacob and Leah.[3] The Midrash explains that Leah our Matriarch chose the name "Dinah" from the word "din" (judgment), because she passed judgment on herself.[3] Leah knew by prophecy that twelve sons, founders of tribes, were destined to be born to Jacob.[3] After she had already borne six sons, and the maidservants had borne four, Leah understood that if she bore a seventh son, her sister Rachel would be left with only one son (fewer than the maidservants).[3] She prayed that the fetus in her womb would become female in order to save her sister's honor, and so Dinah was born.[3] Dinah thus represents the capacity to judge oneself for the sake of another, out of a systemic view of the good of all Israel.[3]
While the Torah does not elaborate on Jacob's other daughters (although the Midrash notes that a twin sister was born with each tribe), Dinah is the only daughter whose story is detailed in the Bible.[3] She stood out in her uniqueness and her virtues.[3] Similarly, Rebbetzin Denah Weinberg stood out in the world of outreach thanks to her original leadership.[3] She did not stand "behind" her great husband, but "stood on her own feet" and paved an independent path for cultivating Jewish women's leadership.[3] Her regal, loving and demanding presence made her students feel precious and vital to the future of the Jewish people.[3]
The EYAHT Midrasha: Vision, Institution and Curriculum
The inspiration for founding the EYAHT midrasha grew out of the recognition of the need for an in-depth framework of study for women, parallel to the revolution that Rabbi Noah Weinberg had brought about among men.[6, 7] Rabbi Weinberg himself encouraged his wife to establish the institution and promised to help with separate fundraising for it.[6, 7] The Rebbetzin sought to create a program that would convey the special essence of the woman's role in Judaism, out of the understanding that national leadership and strength begin with building the home.[6, 7]
In 1982 the first study groups began to operate, and in 1984 the midrasha officially opened in two small ground-floor apartments opposite the Rebbetzin's home on Amrei Bina Street in the Kiryat Sanz neighborhood of Jerusalem.[1, 3] The Rebbetzin chose to call the midrasha "EYAHT," an acronym of the verse from Proverbs 31:30: "A woman who fears the Lord, she shall be praised" (Isha yir'at Hashem hi tit'halal).[1, 3]
Criterion of comparison
The founding stage and Kiryat Sanz (1982/4–2014)
The Romema campus stage and the move online (2014 onward)
Physical structure and campus
Two small ground-floor apartments opposite the Rebbetzin's home; rented guest apartments throughout the neighborhood.[1, 3]
A modern 5-story campus with an area of about 1,430 sq m in the Romema neighborhood [3]; a digital learning infrastructure.[6, 7]
Geographic target audience
Academic and professional women from English-speaking countries.[1, 3]
Outreach to a broad international audience alongside the inclusion of Israeli women in the "Shiviti" program.[6, 7]
Teaching methodology
Intensive frontal lessons, chavrutot (study partnerships) and intimate group study.[4]
Flexible learning tracks, a combination of online courses and personally tailored frontal study.[6, 7]
The midrasha's mission was defined simply: to give women the opportunity, the tools, the knowledge and the passion to make an informed decision about their Jewish lives.[6, 7] The curriculum was distinguished by several intellectual and practical aspects:
Torah study without "decorations": the midrasha's educational philosophy rejected the need for "shop windows" or for softening the content for women with a limited background.[4] The Rebbetzin believed that the Torah in its beauty and its original complexity is comprehensible and attractive to every soul.[4] Therefore, the studies were based on direct and demanding halakha lessons without unnecessary philosophical decorations, an approach that proved itself empowering and uplifting.[4]
Integration of the 48 acquisitions of Torah: the midrasha's flagship program included the method of "48 Ways to Wisdom," based on the Mishnah in Tractate Avot 6:6.[3, 8] The Rebbetzin adapted these principles into a practical methodology for personal development, self-discipline and character building.[3, 8]
Focus on the feminine and family role: alongside the theoretical lessons, the midrasha offered dedicated courses in child-rearing (the education of children) and in shalom bayit (domestic harmony).[3] This content was not taught merely as technical instructions, but as an inseparable part of the theological outlook on the importance of the Jewish home.[3]
In 2014, thanks to fundraising efforts led by the student Bonnie Cohen, the midrasha's splendid permanent campus was inaugurated in the Romema neighborhood.[3, 6, 7] Although in the following years changes took place in the institutional structure, the spirit of Rebbetzin Weinberg continues to pulse through online and frontal lessons, and through the "Shiviti" program, which is intended for Israeli women and continues the midrasha's path of empowering women through Torah.[6, 7]
Her Torah Teaching and Thought
Rebbetzin Weinberg's thought is based on an uncompromising demand for doing justice, striving for Divine truth and requiring personal excellence.[2, 3] Five foundational sayings and intellectual ideas define her teaching [2]:
"It Is Not Enough to Be Good, We Must Be Great"
The Rebbetzin demanded of her students that they realize the full potential hidden within them.[2, 3] She used to say that no one wants the eulogist at their funeral to say: "She was fine, fairly average."[2] Striving for mediocrity was in her eyes a sad waste of the gift of life.[3] She repeated again and again to her students the mantra: "Be a great Jewish woman."[2]
"If Twenty People Are Standing at the Bus Stop and the Bus Does Not Stop, There Are Twenty Different Reasons for It"
This saying reflected her deep belief in individual Divine providence and in the existence of a constant dialectical relationship between the Creator and man.[2] The Rebbetzin taught that every event in reality carries within it a personal and precise message from the Holy One, blessed be He, to each and every individual, and a person must listen and decipher what the Creator is trying to tell him specifically.[2]
"To Know Him Is to Love Him"
The more a person deepens his intellectual and spiritual knowledge of his Creator, the more his love for Him necessarily grows.[2] Understanding the attributes of the Holy One, blessed be He—such as lovingkindness, mercy and forbearance—enables a person to resemble Him, to develop a personal relationship with Him and to find existential meaning.[2] She utterly rejected the passive approach represented by the argument "this is simply my nature," and declared: "That is how you were created—now work on yourself and change."[2]
"The Holy One, Blessed Be He, Loves You"
Out of a brilliant monotheistic analysis, the Rebbetzin explained that the one and only God has no lack or need whatsoever.[2] A perfect being without deficiencies cannot "receive" anything, and therefore its entire essence is absolute giving and pure altruism.[2] Hence, God's love for His creatures is incomparably greater than the love of parents for their children.[2] Family relationships in this world were given to man only to give him a faint and vague notion of the Creator's infinite love for him.[2]
"Your Husband Needs Your Respect"
The Rebbetzin saw mutual respect as the very foundation of a healthy Jewish home.[2] She emphasized that men need respect from their wives as a basic existential need, and that a home in which the wife belittles her husband's worth or his achievements cannot endure.[2] Her practical guidance to women was: "Treat him as a person you respect, and he will become a person you respect."[2]
Her Writing and Written Thought
Alongside her many oral lessons, Rebbetzin Weinberg published a number of essays and articles in anthologies for Jewish women, in which she set out her teaching.[1, 3] Three of her prominent articles present different aspects of her outlook:
Title of the article
The central idea and the spiritual teaching
Application and practical significance
"The Crushed Cake" [9]
Life demands flexibility, gratitude and spiritual proportion; outward perfection is no guarantee of happiness or of true enjoyment.
Just as the crushed cake was the tastiest for the fifth-grade children, so one must learn to appreciate the beauty in the imperfect situations of life.[9, 10]
"Normal Life" [9]
A critique of the modern tendency to try to "understand" and analyze everything in an overly rational way, which harms the simplicity of faith and the acceptance of reality.
A call to others to try to "understand less" and to accept the Creator's will out of acceptance and trust instead of out of intellectual analysis alone.[9]
"Shabbat Candles: Lights of the Soul" [9]
Shabbat is a romantic and spiritual love song between the Congregation of Israel and the Holy One, blessed be He, and the candles are a physical expression of this love.
The Shabbat candles parallel the candles lit at romantic dinners; they are meant to create an atmosphere of deep soul connection within the home.[9]
The Holiness of the Home, Motherhood and Everyday Work
Rebbetzin Weinberg's intellectual contribution stands out especially against the background of the feminist trends of the late twentieth century, which at times tended to present housework and the care of children as an inferior occupation or as an obstacle to personal development.[3] The Rebbetzin created an opposite worldview, which raises the domestic routine to the level of supreme holy service.[3]
A clear example of this is her famous lesson on the spiritual essence of changing a diaper.[3] The Rebbetzin explained that changing a baby's dirty diaper is not merely a physical act, but is in its essence parallel to the process of teshuvah (repentance).[3] The act of cleaning and helping another to be rid of dirt and to start anew is a Divine act of purification and kindness.[3] This understanding gave women the ability to find sublime and deep meaning precisely in the most Sisyphean and routine moments of family life.[3]
She refused to separate the world of the intellect and of lofty thought from the practice of running a home.[4] She proved by her deeds that a woman can raise twelve children, run an international educational institution, lecture throughout the world and counsel thousands of women who turned to her, without giving up her central role as a mother and homemaker.[1, 4] She taught that the strength and leadership of the Jewish woman are not measured by media noise or by external power struggles, but by the ability to influence people's souls deeply and intimately and to build a family unit founded on Torah truth.[3, 6, 7]
Summary and Legacy
The work and Torah teaching of Rebbetzin Denah Weinberg represent a unique combination of halakhic depth, rigorous self-discipline and abundant human warmth.[4] She succeeded in breaking through the accepted boundaries of the world of outreach to women through a persistent demand for direct and in-depth Torah study, without compromises and without resorting to easy solutions.[4] The EYAHT midrasha that she founded created an unprecedented network of educated and committed women, who integrated into their communities as influencers and leaders.[3, 6, 7]
Through her thought, the Rebbetzin succeeded in illuminating everyday life with the light of holiness, and in proving that motherhood and building the home are the most powerful tools for tikkun olam (repairing the world) and for connecting to the Creator.[3] Her death in 2023 marked the end of the era of the founders of the modern teshuvah movement, but her educational and Torah legacy continues to guide her students and graduates, who continue to walk on the path she charted towards spiritual greatness and meaningful action for the sake of the community.[2, 4]
